```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: true
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk <- load_walk()
```

These exercises build the vocabulary and intuition of Module 1: classifying designs, taking a dataset apart, separating between- from within-person variation, writing estimands and seeing by simulation what goes wrong when repeated measurements are treated as independent. Guided exercises have partly completed code with blanks (`___`) and questions to answer in words. Independent exercises give a task with no scaffolding. Simulations are kept small so that they run in a minute or two; say how many replicates you used whenever you report a simulation result.

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

## Guided exercises

### Exercise 1. Classifying designs (LO 1.1)

Classify each design as cross-sectional, repeated measures without a time axis, longitudinal, clustered, or a combination. For each, name the independent unit and justify your answer in one or two sentences.

a. A national survey measures blood pressure once in 5,000 randomly selected adults.
b. In one session, each of 40 volunteers has blood pressure measured in three postures (lying, sitting, standing), in random order.
c. A trial randomises 30 general practices to a new or usual care pathway and measures HbA1c once in 20 patients per practice.
d. 300 adults with chronic kidney disease have eGFR measured at routine clinic visits for up to 5 years (KIDNEY).
e. 200 participants in the CLEAR trial rate their itch at weeks 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12.
f. The WALK trial: 360 participants at 8 clinics, SBP at months 0, 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12.

### Exercise 2. Anatomy of a dataset (LO 1.2, 1.4)

a. For WALK, name the variable that identifies the subject, the variable that identifies the visit, and the variable that holds the measurement occasion. What is one observation?
b. Run `check_long()` on WALK and count observations per participant.

```{r}
#| eval: false
check_long(walk, ___, month_sched, "sbp")
walk |> count(___, name = "n_obs") |> count(n_obs)
```

c. Summarise how far actual visit times deviate from the schedule at each visit. At which visit are deviations largest?

```{r}
#| eval: false
walk |>
  mutate(deviation = ___ - ___) |>
  group_by(month_sched) |>
  summarise(sd_dev = sd(deviation), max_abs_dev = max(abs(deviation)))
```

d. Load CLEAR, DIARY and KIDNEY (`load_clear()`, `load_diary()`, `load_kidney()`). For each, identify the subject, the time variable, and whether there is a distinction between scheduled and actual time. In DIARY, what is a "measurement occasion"?
e. Which of the four datasets is closest to balanced? Which has the most unequal follow-up?

### Exercise 3. Between- and within-person variation (LO 1.3)

a. Compute the observed correlation matrix of SBP across scheduled visits, separately in each arm.

```{r}
#| eval: false
for (a in levels(walk$arm)) {
  print(a)
  print(round(visit_correlation(filter(walk, arm == ___), id, month_sched, sbp), 2))
}
```

Describe the pattern in words. Is it similar across arms?

b. Fit the random-intercept model with visit-by-arm fixed effects and extract the variance components and the ICC.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m_ri <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 | ___), data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
VarCorr(m_ri)
icc_lmer(___)
```

c. Interpret the between-participant SD, the residual SD and the ICC in words and in mmHg.
d. Refit with no fixed effects except an intercept (`sbp ~ 1 + (1 | id)`). Which variance component changes most, and why?
e. The ICC of the random-intercept model is a single number. Compare it with the observed correlations from part a. What does the model get right and what does it miss?

### Exercise 4. Research questions and estimands (LO 1.5)

For each question, say whether it is about change, a group difference in change or individual trajectories, and write the estimand using the notation of the notes ($\mu_{\text{arm}}(t)$ for the mean SBP in an arm at month $t$, $b_{1i}$ for an individual slope deviation).

a. By how much does mean SBP fall between baseline and month 6 in the standard programme?
b. Is the reduction in SBP from baseline to month 12 larger in the enhanced programme than in the standard programme?
c. How much do WALK participants differ in their rate of change in SBP over the year?
d. In KIDNEY, do people with diabetes lose kidney function faster than people without diabetes?
e. A colleague writes: "SBP fell significantly in EP (p < 0.001) but not in usual care (p = 0.2), so the programme works." What estimand should they have used, and why is their argument flawed?

### Exercise 5. A small simulation (LO 1.6)

Run a reduced version of the scenario A simulation from the notes with 200 replicates.

```{r}
#| eval: false
sim_once <- function() {
  d <- sim_two_arm(n_per_arm = 50, times = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12), b0 = 150,
                   b_time = -0.5, delta = 0, sd_int = 11, sd_slope = 0,
                   cor_int_slope = 0, sd_resid = 6)
  ols <- coef(summary(lm(y ~ time + trt, data = d)))
  lmm <- coef(summary(lmer(y ~ time + trt + (1 | id), data = d, control = lmer_ctrl)))
  c(arm_est = ols["trt", 1], arm_se_ols = ols["trt", 2], arm_se_lmm = lmm["trt", 2],
    time_est = ols["time", 1], time_se_ols = ols["time", 2], time_se_lmm = lmm["time", 2])
}
set.seed(___)
res <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(___, sim_once())))
c(sd_arm = sd(res$arm_est), ols = mean(res$arm_se_ols), lmm = mean(res$arm_se_lmm))
c(sd_time = sd(res$time_est), ols = mean(res$time_se_ols), lmm = mean(res$time_se_lmm))
```

a. Compare the average OLS and mixed-model SEs with the empirical SD of the estimates, for the arm difference and for the time slope. In which direction is each OLS SE wrong?
b. Compute the Monte Carlo SE of each empirical SD ($\text{SD}/\sqrt{2(R-1)}$). Are your conclusions secure given this error?
c. Compute the coverage of nominal 95% OLS intervals for the arm difference (true value 0). What does this imply about the false-positive rate of a naive test?
d. Explain in plain words why the two OLS errors go in opposite directions.

## Independent exercises

### Exercise 6. Balance and follow-up in CLEAR and DIARY (LO 1.2, 1.4)

Describe the structure of CLEAR and DIARY: number of subjects and observations, distribution of observations per subject, and whether the occasions are fixed. In DIARY, the exposure (`days` with a completed diary) varies between periods: explain why this is a form of imbalance even when every period is present, and what a model would need to do about it.

### Exercise 7. Variance components in KIDNEY (LO 1.3)

Fit a random-intercept model for eGFR in KIDNEY with fixed effects for `years` and `diabetes`. Report the between- and within-person SDs and the ICC, and interpret them. Give one reason why the random-intercept model is probably too simple for these data, and one reason why an ICC from these data should be interpreted with care given how visits were scheduled.

### Exercise 8. Naive and mixed-model SEs in WALK (LO 1.6)

Fit `lm(sbp ~ month + sex)` and `lmer(sbp ~ month + sex + (1 | id))` to WALK. Compare the standard errors for `month` and `sexFemale`. Explain the direction of each difference using the ideas of between- and within-subject comparisons.

### Exercise 9. When individual slopes vary a lot (LO 1.6)

Modify `sim_once_rs()` from the notes so that you can vary `sd_slope`. With 200 replicates each, run scenario B with `sd_slope` equal to 0.4, 1.5 and 3. For each, compare the OLS and mixed-model SEs of the arm-by-time interaction with the empirical SD. Describe how the direction of the OLS error depends on how much individual slopes vary, and explain why.
